segments.text: We're the first humans to fly the spacecraft, and our first action can be right and it can save our lives, or it could be really wrong, and that could really hurt us.
So, we develop like no fast hands in the cockpit, like go slow, let's be cerebral and methodical about our decisions.
But at the end of the day, if there is an emergency that needs an immediate action, something that must happen right now, we develop the mantra of what is the first right thing you need to do.
And if you do that first right thing,
You generally can get yourself out of most of those main issues.
And so that was really what we went through every time we were faced with a challenge.
What's the first right thing?
Let's go slow and methodical.
Let's try to figure out what's going on with the vehicle, what's going on in Houston, and let's talk through this.
And we didn't have a whole lot of major emergencies on this mission.
And everything that we did have pretty much turned out to be a false alarm.
So maybe we weren't challenged sufficiently, but.
That's a long answer to a short question.
I think that you were challenged more than enough and you executed well as a team.
And one of the best parts about being a captain on a ship is actually having your shipmates work with you.
And that's collaboration.
Yeah.
I love them.
That's wonderful.
So now everyone has talked about how successful the Artemis II mission was, how much we accomplished, how much we learned, how much we may have increased efficiencies.
So, tell us something about the Artemis II mission that the public may not know happened.
Oh, it was so hard to get to our food.
We had this amazing food.
We had like the best space food that any astronauts have ever eaten in space from our food lab here at Johnson Space Center.
But it was just, it was very hard for us to get.
To the food in the way you would want to eat.
They're just in these large bags, and breakfast is mashed in with lunch, which is mashed in with dinner.
And so we had these great menus, but in the end of the day, you're floating, and we had no way to store all this food that was coming out of this bag.
There's like, think if you pack for a long trip and maybe you use one of those compression pockets where they take all the air out.
So three days' worth of clothes fits into like a baseball glove, you know, backpack.
So, think about that.
And now, think about removing gravity and your weightless.
And you take scissors and you cut open that backpack.
And now, all that force is there, and everything that's in that backpack now is expanding.
Well, think if it's 10 days' worth of food, or in our case, three days' worth of food.
That's a tremendous amount of packaging and food products that we just didn't have anywhere to store.
We didn't have little Ziplocs, we didn't have ways to organize, we didn't have ways to dig in and find all this food.
So we were really behind the timeline the first few days as these four humans are in this small vehicle living.
It's a magnificent vehicle.
And once we hit our stride towards the end of the mission, it was very easy to work and live in there and very comfortable.
But those first few days, I think the thing that was just getting to me the most was food.
And then maybe.
A little bit of Outlook inefficiencies based on how we're using the deep space network with Outlook.
Like I joked that with my kids, they would get my response to two days ago's email today because we would only get a sync once twice a day.
So they would email me.
I wouldn't, I would get that on the next sync.
I would reply on the next sync, and then they would get it on the next sync.
So that's like 48 hours from the time they email me until they get anything back.
And so, think about how out of sorts we were.
Like, I'm trying to answer questions from Monday, but it's Wednesday.
And then on Friday, they're reading my answers on Wednesday to their Monday email.
That's like longer than a comm delay from here to Mars.
By far.
So, anyway, that I mean, that led to some humor, but it was just an honor that we even had.
